source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 4

overview.bigIdea: For most people, **democracy = political parties**. Parties contest elections, make policies, form governments and oppose them. They are not always trusted – but modern democracy cannot work without them. The chapter asks: why parties, how many, which ones, and how to fix them?

ladder.a: Seven functions; necessary for representative democracy
Four challenges; reforms made and suggested

languages.name: 7 functions
languages.text: Contest, policies, laws, govern, oppose, opinion, access.

languages.name: 4 challenges
languages.text: Internal democracy, dynasty, money & muscle, no real choice.

plan.text: Lesson 1 – learn the seven functions with the match game.
Lessons 2–3 – party systems; one fact per national party.
Lesson 4 – sort challenges, reforms made and suggestions.
Check knowledge quiz; revise after 1, 3 and 7 days.

lessons.title: Why do we need political parties?
lessons.hook: Imagine an election where every candidate is independent. Each promises to fix the local road – but **no one can promise how the country will be run**. That missing piece is exactly what political parties provide.

core.def: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government, agreeing on policies and programmes to promote the collective good.
The leaders, the active members and the followers.
Parties are about a part of society; a partisan is strongly committed to a party and unable to take a balanced view.

1 Contest elections · 2 Put forward policies and programmes · 3 Make laws · 4 Form and run governments · 5 Play opposition · 6 Shape public opinion · 7 Provide access to government machinery and welfare schemes.
Parties are linked to representative democracy: large societies need an agency to gather views, support or restrain the government, and make responsible government possible.

explain: Candidates: in the USA, members and supporters choose them; in India, top party leaders choose them.
Even ‘non-party’ panchayat elections split villages into factions that put up panels – which is what parties do. That is why almost every country has parties.

example.q: State the various functions political parties perform in a democracy. (5 marks)
steps: **Contest elections** – put up candidates (chosen by top leaders in India).
**Put forward policies and programmes** – reduce many opinions into a few basic positions for voters to choose from.
**Make laws** – members in the legislature follow the party leadership.
**Form and run governments / act as opposition** – recruit and train leaders; losing parties criticise and mobilise opposition.
**Shape public opinion and provide access** – raise issues, launch movements, help citizens reach government schemes.
example.answer: Seven functions grouped into five points.

mistakes: Confusing parties with pressure groups (pressure groups do not contest elections).
Saying parties choose candidates the same way everywhere.
lessons.tip: Use the memory hook to write all seven functions in order – examiners count them.
lessons.memory: C-P-L-G-O-O-A: Contest, Policies, Laws, Govern, Oppose, Opinion, Access.

cards.q: Why can’t democracy work without parties?
cards.a: No one could promise policies or be responsible for running the country.

lessons.title: How many parties should we have?
lessons.hook: China has one party, the USA mostly two, India hundreds. Which is best? The chapter’s surprising answer: **it is not a very good question** – a party system grows out of a country’s society and history.

core.def: Only one party is allowed to control and run the government, e.g. China (Communist Party). Not a democratic option.
Power usually changes between two main parties, e.g. USA and UK.
Several parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power, alone or in alliance, e.g. India.
Parties join hands to contest elections and win power – in 2004: NDA, UPA and Left Front.
Trust in parties is low all over the world, but in India party membership (higher than Canada, Japan, Spain, South Korea) and closeness to parties have gone up.

explain: More than 750 parties are registered with the Election Commission of India, but only a handful are serious contenders.
A multiparty system can look messy and unstable, but it lets a variety of interests and opinions be represented – which suits India’s social and geographical diversity.

example.q: ‘Party system is not something any country can choose.’ Explain. (3 marks)
steps: A party system evolves over a long time depending on the nature of society, its social and regional divisions, its history of politics and its system of elections.
These cannot be changed very quickly; each country develops a system conditioned by its special circumstances.
India has a multiparty system because its social and geographical diversity is not easily absorbed by two or three parties. No system is ideal for all countries.
example.answer: Evolves with society · cannot change quickly · India’s diversity → multiparty.

mistakes: Saying a one-party system can be democratic.
lessons.tip: For party-system answers: define it, give one country example, and one advantage or problem.
examAsk: Types of party systems with examples.
Why has India a multiparty system?

lessons.title: National and State parties
lessons.hook: Every party must register with the Election Commission, but only big, established parties get a **unique symbol** that only their official candidates can use. Getting that recognition needs a minimum share of votes and seats.

core.def: State party: at least 6% of votes in a State assembly election and at least 2 seats. National party: at least 6% of votes in Lok Sabha or assembly elections in four States and at least 4 Lok Sabha seats.
Aam Aadmi Party, Bharatiya Janata Party, Bahujan Samaj Party, CPI(M), Indian National Congress, National People’s Party.

INC: 1885, centrist, dominant for decades after Independence. BJP: 1980 (reviving the Bharatiya Jana Sangh of 1951, Syama Prasad Mukherjee); integral humanism and Antyodaya (Deendayal Upadhyaya); 303 seats in 2019.

BSP: 1984, Kanshi Ram, bahujan samaj; inspired by Sahu Maharaj, Phule, Periyar, Ambedkar; base in Uttar Pradesh. CPI(M): 1964, Marxism-Leninism; strong in West Bengal (34 years in power), Kerala, Tripura.
AAP: 26 November 2012, after the 2011 anti-corruption movement; governments in Delhi and Punjab. NPP: July 2013, P.A. Sangma; first North-East party to become national; government in Meghalaya.

explain: **State parties** (commonly called regional parties) need not be regional in outlook: e.g. Samajwadi Party, Rashtriya Janata Dal; others like Biju Janata Dal, Sikkim Democratic Front, Mizo National Front are conscious of State identity.
Since 1996, nearly every State party has been part of a national coalition government – strengthening federalism and democracy.

example.q: Describe any three national parties of India. (3 marks)
steps: **Indian National Congress:** founded 1885; one of the oldest parties in the world; centrist; secularism and welfare of weaker sections.
**Bharatiya Janata Party:** founded 1980 reviving the Bharatiya Jana Sangh; inspired by integral humanism and Antyodaya; won 303 seats in 2019.
**Bahujan Samaj Party:** formed 1984 under Kanshi Ram; represents dalits, adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities; main base Uttar Pradesh.
example.answer: Three parties, each with year + leader/idea + one fact.

mistakes: Mixing up BSP’s founder (Kanshi Ram) with its inspirations (Ambedkar, Phule).
Saying there are seven national parties – the 2023 list has six.
Thinking all State parties have a regional ideology.
lessons.tip: Learn one ‘year + idea’ tag per national party – that is enough for most 1- and 3-mark questions.

lessons.title: Challenges and reforms
lessons.hook: People blame parties for whatever goes wrong in democracy. The chapter narrows the criticism to **four problems** – and shows what has been done, what is suggested, and why citizens themselves matter.

core.def: Power concentrated in one or a few leaders; no membership registers, meetings or internal elections; personal loyalty to the leader matters more.
Few ways for ordinary workers to rise; top posts controlled by one family – unfair and bad for democracy.
Parties nominate candidates who can raise money; rich people and companies influence policies; sometimes criminals are supported.
Declining ideological differences (e.g. Labour and Conservative in Britain); the same leaders shift between parties.
Anti-defection law (constitutional amendment) · Supreme Court: affidavit of property and criminal cases · Election Commission: organisational elections and income tax returns.

explain: **Suggestions not yet accepted:** a law to regulate internal affairs (member registers, own constitution, independent authority, open elections); one-third of tickets to women and a quota in decision-making bodies; state funding of elections.

**Be careful with legal solutions:** over-regulation can make parties cheat the law. Two other ways: **people’s pressure** (petitions, publicity, agitations, media) and **more people joining parties** – ‘bad politics can be solved by more and better politics’.

example.q: Suggest some reforms to strengthen political parties so that they perform their functions well. (5 marks)
steps: **Anti-defection law:** MLAs and MPs who change parties lose their seats – this has reduced defection.
**Affidavits:** candidates must declare property and criminal cases – making information public.
**Internal democracy:** the Election Commission requires organisational elections and tax returns; a law could require member registers and open elections.
**Women and money:** one-third of tickets for women; state funding of elections to reduce the role of money.
**Citizens:** public pressure through petitions, media and agitations, and more people joining parties.
example.answer: Laws already made + suggestions + role of citizens.

mistakes: Confusing a challenge with a reform.
Forgetting the downside of the anti-defection law (dissent harder).
Writing only legal solutions without people’s pressure.
lessons.tip: Structure reform answers as: Made → Suggested → Citizens. Three blocks, five points.
lessons.memory: Challenges: I-D-M-C (Internal democracy, Dynasty, Money & muscle, Choice).

revision: A political party contests elections and holds power; components: leaders, active members, followers.
Seven functions: contest elections, policies, laws, form and run governments, opposition, public opinion, access to government.
Parties are necessary for representative democracy; without them no one is responsible for running the country.
One-party (China), two-party (USA, UK), multiparty (India); alliances: NDA, UPA, Left Front (2004).
A party system evolves with society; India’s diversity produced a multiparty system.
Trust in parties is low, but party membership in India is high and rising.
Recognition: State party 6% votes + 2 assembly seats; national party 6% in Lok Sabha or 4 States + 4 Lok Sabha seats.
Six national parties (2023): AAP, BJP, BSP, CPI(M), INC, NPP.
Four challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, no meaningful choice.
Reforms: anti-defection law, affidavits, EC orders; suggestions: internal affairs law, 1/3 tickets to women, state funding; people’s pressure.

sections.title: Party answers · 4 steps
items: List the functions, challenges or reforms as numbered points.
Add one Indian example per point (NDA, anti-defection, affidavit).
Close with a judgement (parties are necessary but need reform).

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line definition or introduction using textbook keywords (e.g. ‘Majoritarianism is …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, with the key term in the first few words. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a real example from the chapter to each point (Belgium, Sri Lanka, Panchayati Raj, a party, a survey figure).
Use the exact numbers the textbook gives only when you are sure (59%, 1956, 1992, one-third, 1976).
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ questions use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Distinguish’ questions draw a small two-column table.
Case-based questions: underline the key line in the passage first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn sorts – if you can sort every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can define a political party and name its three components.
I can write all seven functions.
I can explain the three party systems with examples.
I can describe three national parties with facts.
I can list four challenges, three reforms made and three suggestions.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark case/source-based and 5-mark long answers). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
